stops.name: Mecca and Medina, the second hajj
stops.campa: Nearly forty years after the first pilgrimage with his father, Abd al-Qadir returns to the Hijaz, spending three months in Taif and eight in Mecca in the company of a Darqawi shaykh, Muhammad al-Fasi al-Shadhili, before three further months at Medina. He is no longer the boy marked without knowing it; he is a general, a statesman, and now, in the eyes of the Muslim world entire, a saint who armed his household to save Christians. The hajj he makes now is the hajj of a man who has already lived out, in blood and captivity and rescue, whatever the first journey planted in him.

stops.name: Alexandria, initiated into Freemasonry
stops.campa: French Freemasons of the Henri IV lodge in Paris, moved by the rescue of 1860, had approached him within weeks of the Damascus events; four years later the Alexandria lodge Les Pyramides d'Égypte initiates him formally on the Paris lodge's behalf, confirmed the following year in Paris itself. He leaves within a year, troubled, his circle records, by a drift among some brothers away from belief in God and the soul's survival. The episode marks the width of his fame: honored by an institution his own students never imagined him entering, and left on the same terms of conscience that governed him at Sidi Brahim and in the Christian quarter.

stops.name: Port Said, the opening of the Suez Canal
stops.campa: Ferdinand de Lesseps and the Khedive Ismail Pasha invite the old emir among the sovereigns and dignitaries of the world to witness the canal opened between two seas. In the crowd of Europe's royalty he meets another old enemy of empire, Imam Shamil of the Caucasus, defeated by Russia as he was defeated by France; the two resistance leaders, who fought the same century's great powers a continent apart, recognize each other at a glance and speak long into the evening of wars fought and lost and outlived.

stops.name: Damascus, the last years of the Mawaqif
stops.campa: In old age his day keeps the shape the zawiya gave it seventy years before: two hours of prayer and meditation before sunrise, the morning at his correspondence, midday prayer at the mosque, three hours teaching his circle the sciences of Ibn Arabi, evenings with his sons — he will father some thirty children in his lifetime — and a monthly distribution of not less than four thousand francs to the city's poor. The Kitab al-Mawaqif grows by dictation, meditation on meditation, until it fills volumes; visitors from Europe and the Islamic world alike come to the Amara house to sit at the feet of the soldier-saint and leave, by their own accounts, uncertain which title fits him better.

stops.name: Damascus, death in the house at Amara
stops.campa: In the night of the twenty-fifth to the twenty-sixth of May Abd al-Qadir dies in his house behind the Umayyad Mosque, seventy-four years old, fifty-seven years to the season since he first knelt as a pilgrim boy at the tomb of Ibn Arabi and could not have known he would end his life a street away from it. The city that received him as an exile buries him as one of its own great shaykhs, and the French government that fought him for seventeen years and imprisoned him for five sends its condolences as to a head of state.

stops.name: Salihiyya, buried beside the Shaykh al-Akbar
stops.campa: He is laid in the ground beside Ibn Arabi, at his own long-declared wish, closing a circuit begun by an eighteen-year-old pilgrim who prayed at this same tomb not knowing what his life would hold: war, statehood, capture, five years of French prisons, exile, and a single week in July when he stood between a mob and thousands of strangers of another faith because his own law told him to. In 1966, independent Algeria will ask for his remains and his family will grant them, and he will be moved to the martyrs' cemetery of El Alia above Algiers — but Damascus, and Ibn Arabi's company, was the resting place he himself chose.
